quartiers:The palace.name: The palace
quartiers:The palace.teaser: Four Roman gates, one colonnaded court, and washing lines strung between 1,700-year-old walls
quartiers:The palace.story: Diocletian built this as his retirement house; when Salona fell in the 7th century its people moved inside the walls and never left. Today you enter by one of four gates: Golden to the north, Silver to the east by the Pazar, Bronze from the sea, Iron to the west. All four lanes lead to the Peristyle, where red granite columns frame the cathedral steps. One alley off, the palace turns domestic: a scooter against a Roman pilaster, laundry over a medieval window. How many still live here is argued: 3,000 is the usual figure, Fodor's says just over 1,000 and falling as flats become rentals.
quartiers:The palace.why: Walk it twice: once at first light, empty, and once after the cruise passengers have gone back aboard.
facts: The Roman gates, the Peristyle, and the lanes where people still hang their washing
Before 08:30 or after dark; on cruise days the lanes jam from mid-morning (see 'The cruise-day midday')
The Silver Gate side, where the Pazar spills up to the wall; the Peristyle late at night, with its sphinx
Bokeria Kitchen & Wine, Šug, Villa Spiza, Apetit
Residents: about 3,000 (Wikipedia and older guides) against more than 1,000 and shrinking (Fodor's); no census figure found (Oct 2026)

quartiers:Veli Varoš.name: Veli Varoš
quartiers:Veli Varoš.teaser: Steep stone lanes west of the palace, where Split's fishermen lived and the konobas still cook
quartiers:Veli Varoš.story: West of the Riva the streets tilt up toward Marjan. Veli Varoš grew outside the walls around the little church of St Nicholas, Sveti Mikula, which the tourist board calls perhaps the best preserved medieval church in Split; the hamlet then was Stagnja. Until recently this was the fishermen's quarter: low stone houses, outside stairs, lanes too narrow and steep for a car. The parish of the Holy Cross, Sveti Križ, has kept its feast on 14 September for some six centuries. It is also a byword for the fetivi, the old Split families with their famously fast talk, as against boduli from the islands and vlaji from the hinterland.
quartiers:Veli Varoš.why: Come for dinner and arrive an hour early: the lanes before the meal are half the reason to eat here.
facts: Stone houses, steep stairs up to Marjan, and the city's family konobas
Early evening, on the way up to dinner

quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.name: The Riva and Matejuška
quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.teaser: Palms, white paving and the palace's sea wall, ending at a harbour full of small wooden fishing boats
quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.story: The Riva runs along the palace's south wall, where the sea once lapped the Bronze Gate. Its central stretch was rebuilt in 2006-2007; the digging turned up a Roman sea wall and landing platform in front of the palace. Behind the cafés, the Prokurative (Trg Republike) opens to the water through neo-Renaissance arcades on three sides, begun in 1859 with a theatre at its centre that burned in 1882. At the western end the paving gives way to Matejuška, the fishermen's harbour, where small wooden boats are pulled up on the stone and men mend nets. The ferries for Brač and Hvar pull out across the bay.
quartiers:The Riva and Matejuška.why: Use it as the city's hallway: coffee on the Riva, then walk to the end of it and sit at Matejuška.
facts: The palace's sea face, the arcaded Prokurative, and the working boats at Matejuška
Early morning for coffee; the evening walk, when the city comes out

quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.name: Bačvice and Firule
quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.teaser: Sand underfoot ten minutes from the palace, then a quieter pine-backed bay where locals swim
quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.story: Walk east past the ferry and cruise terminal and the city opens onto its own beaches. Bačvice comes first: a sandy, shallow bay, rare on a coast of pebbles, with bars and terraces stacked above the water and the shallows where picigin is played. Beyond it lies Ovčice, a pebble strip with beach bars, then Firule, a sandy cove under pines that draws families and Split people more than visitors. Above Firule's water sits Dvor and its terrace. In late autumn several beach bars close or cut their hours from November: check the season.
quartiers:Bačvice and Firule.why: Swim at Bačvice for the scene, walk on to Firule for the quiet, and stay for dinner at Dvor.
facts: Sand in the city, the bars above Bačvice, and the quieter cove at Firule
Early morning for an empty beach; late afternoon to watch picigin

curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.name: The sphinx on the Peristyle
curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.teaser: A black granite sphinx about 3,500 years old, brought from Egypt by the emperor and still on guard
curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.story: Most visitors photograph the columns and walk past it. Low against the cathedral side of the Peristyle lies a black granite sphinx, about two and a half metres long, carved in Egypt in the 15th century BC and usually linked to Thutmose III. Diocletian had put down a revolt in Egypt around 297 and shipped home a dozen or more sphinxes to line his new palace. Only a few survive: this one, a headless one in front of the Temple of Jupiter, and a third in the City Museum. Who smashed the rest is not recorded.
curiosities:The sphinx on the peristyle.why: It is older than Rome itself: put a hand on the oldest object in the city.
facts: Come after 23:30 on a November night, when the terraces have packed up: sit on the steps under the Vestibule, and the granite is cold and the court is silent

Pharaoh: Thutmose III in most accounts, Thutmose I in some. Numbers: twelve sphinxes in one account, fragments of 13 in another. The '3,500 years in Split' line mixes the carving date with the arrival, which was about 1,700 years ago

curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.name: Grgur Ninski's toe
curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.teaser: Rub the bishop's big toe, not his thumb: the bronze has been polished gold by millions of hands
curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.story: Outside the Golden Gate a bronze bishop some eight metres tall raises his finger at the sky. Ivan Meštrović made Grgur Ninski in 1929 for the medieval bishop of Nin who fought for the Slavonic liturgy against Latin, and first set him in the middle of the Peristyle. During the Second World War he was taken down, and only in the 1950s was he raised again outside the palace's north gate. The custom is to rub his big toe for luck, and the toe now shines bright gold against the dark green bronze. Several guidebooks still say thumb: it is the toe.
curiosities:Grgur Ninski's toe.why: Make a wish on the toe on your way in through the Golden Gate.
facts: Rub the big toe of the left foot, then walk through the Golden Gate into the palace
Who removed it in 1941 (the Italian occupiers or the wartime Croatian state) and when it returned (1954 or 1957); the height is given as anything from 7.6 m to 8.5 m

curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.name: No flies in the fish hall
curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.teaser: A hall full of fresh fish in summer, and, so Split insists, not a single fly
curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.story: Stand by the Ribarnica, Peškarija in dialect, on a July morning and notice what is missing: the flies. The story every Splićanin will tell you is that the sulphur springs next door keep them off. The springs are real. The Art Nouveau spa building of 1903 at the end of Marmontova stands over waters used as a cure since the 18th century, and on some days you can smell them. Local lore even claims the springs drew Diocletian here. Whether sulphur actually keeps insects out of a fish market is another matter: we found the claim repeated, never tested.
curiosities:No flies in the fish hall.why: Go early, look and sniff for yourself: the fish is the reason, the riddle is a bonus.
facts: Walk from the fish stalls to the old sulphur spa a few steps away and see whether you smell it
The springs and the spa are documented; that they keep the flies away is local legend, repeated by travel pages and never shown

curiosities:The stone of the White House.name: The stone of the White House
curiosities:The stone of the White House.teaser: Brač stone built Diocletian's palace. Whether it ever reached Washington is another story
curiosities:The stone of the White House.story: Every guide on this coast tells you the White House is built of Brač stone. It was not. Its walls were raised in 1792-1799 from Aquia Creek sandstone, quarried in Virginia and painted white. The Brač version shrinks on inspection to a claim that island stone went into a 1902 renovation, or into a fireplace, backed by a shipping receipt nobody cites; the islanders say the quarry records were destroyed in the war. The palace you are standing in is different: Split's City Museum says it was built almost entirely of Brač limestone, cut near Škrip and shipped from Splitska.
curiosities:The stone of the White House.why: Trust the palace wall under your hand, not the Washington story.
facts: Lay a palm on the palace's south wall on the Riva: that pale stone came across the channel from Brač 1,700 years ago
Aquia Creek sandstone for the White House is documented (USGS). Brač stone for a 1902 renovation or a fireplace rests on promotional pages; the Reichstag claim we could not trace at all

curiosities:Picigin.name: Picigin
curiosities:Picigin.teaser: Knee-deep water, a small ball, and one rule: it must never touch the sea
curiosities:Picigin.story: At Bačvice grown men dive full length into knee-deep water to save a ball. That is picigin: players stand in a loose ring and slap a small ball to one another with the flat of the hand, and the only rule that matters is that it must not land in the sea. There is no score and no winner, only the save. It was first played here in 1908, the story goes, by students home from university who found water polo hopeless in such shallow water. In 2013 Croatia's Ministry of Culture listed it as intangible heritage, and Bačvice hosts a picigin world championship.
curiosities:Picigin.why: Watch one late-afternoon game: the dives into ankle-deep water are the point.
facts: Stand at the water's edge at Bačvice on a warm afternoon; in late October games are rarer, but locals still play on mild days
1908 and Bačvice in most accounts; a family history in a folklore archive puts the start in the 1920s

culture:The substructures.name: The substructures
culture:The substructures.teaser: The emperor's floor plan, preserved in the dark: vaulted halls where Daenerys kept her dragons
culture:The substructures.story: Diocletian's apartments stood above the sea on a vaulted cellar storey that copied the rooms above, hall for hall. The apartments are gone; the cellars are almost entirely preserved and show the emperor's plan in cool, damp stone: long vaulted halls, dripping water, the smell of wet limestone. The central passage from the Bronze Gate is free, lined with stalls; the side halls are ticketed. Game of Thrones used them in season 4 as the vaults where Daenerys chains her dragons. The palace, 215 by 180 metres, built 295-305, is UNESCO-listed since 1979.
culture:The substructures.why: Pay for the side halls: they are the only place to see the emperor's lost apartments laid out room by room.
facts: Under the palace; enter from the Riva through the Bronze Gate or down from the Peristyle

culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.name: The cathedral and its bell tower
culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.teaser: The emperor built himself a tomb; the city turned it into a cathedral for a bishop he had executed
culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.story: Diocletian, persecutor of Christians, built this octagonal mausoleum for himself. Domnius, bishop of Salona, was executed in 304 under him, as tradition records it. In the 7th century the refugees from Salona consecrated the emperor's tomb to Domnius, now Split's patron, Sveti Duje. Andrija Buvina carved the wooden doors in 1214. The Romanesque bell tower, about 57 metres, was heavily restored in 1890-1908; its stairs reopened in 2020 after two years of repair. From the top the Roman grid of the palace is still plain, with Mosor (1,339 m) behind.
culture:The cathedral and its bell tower.why: Climb the tower early: the palace's Roman street grid reads clearly only from above.
facts: On the Peristyle, in the centre of the palace
Seasonal hours, shorter from November; Oct 2026 listings conflict, so check at the ticket desk on the Peristyle

culture:The Archaeological Museum.name: The Archaeological Museum
culture:The Archaeological Museum.teaser: Croatia's oldest museum, founded 1820: Salona's sarcophagi arranged around a quiet garden courtyard
culture:The Archaeological Museum.story: Most of what Salona left behind came here. Founded in 1820 and usually called the oldest museum in Croatia, it keeps its best pieces outdoors in a courtyard lapidarium under arcades: Roman tombstones, inscriptions and two marble sarcophagi from the Manastirine cemetery at Salona, both from the early 4th century. One shows the Greek myth of Hippolytus and Phaedra; the other, the Good Shepherd, puts Christ as a shepherd at its centre, made for Salona's newly Christian elite. Inside are finds from Greek Issa on Vis and the Illyrian hinterland. It is a short walk north of the palace and rarely crowded.
culture:The Archaeological Museum.why: Go for the two Salona sarcophagi, then go to Salona itself and see where they were dug up.
facts: October to May: Monday to Friday 09:00-14:00 and 15:00-20:00, Saturday 09:00-14:00; closed Sunday and holidays (Oct 2026); last entry an hour before closing

culture:Galerija Meštrović.name: Galerija Meštrović
culture:Galerija Meštrović.teaser: The sculptor built his house on Marjan's sea front; then he lost it to the war
culture:Galerija Meštrović.story: Ivan Meštrović (1883-1962), the sculptor behind Grgur Ninski at the Golden Gate, finished this villa on the slope of Marjan in 1939 as a summer house and workshop, with a garden of bronzes falling toward the sea. Today it is a museum holding his marble and bronze figures, reliefs and drawings. A short walk west on the same road, the Kaštilac (Crikvine) holds a chapel lined with his cycle of wooden reliefs of the life of Christ; one ticket covers both.
culture:Galerija Meštrović.why: Walk on to the Kaštilac: the wooden life of Christ in that small chapel is the strongest thing he made.
facts: Šetalište Ivana Meštrovića 46, at the foot of Marjan, about a 15-minute walk west of the centre
Tuesday to Sunday 09:00-17:00, closed Monday and holidays; Kaštilac Tuesday to Sunday 08:00-18:00 (Oct 2026). An energy renovation is under way: check whether the indoor galleries are open
